source_user: A sparse MoE service has uneven expert load and tail latency. Analyze likely causes and experiments. Scenario variant 3: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure routing distribution, expert capacity overflow, all-to-all time, token dropping/padding, placement, batch composition, and compare routing/capacity policies.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: compare the same model, expert count, top-k routing, precision, request mix, sequence lengths, concurrency, and hardware; define tail latency as request-level p95/p99 and treat dropped tokens as quality failures. A falsifiable hypothesis is: if skewed routing or expert capacity overflow is the dominant cause, then reducing max expert load with a tested routing/capacity policy at matched offered load will lower overflow and p99 latency without reducing quality or goodput; if p99 does not improve, the bottleneck is likely elsewhere.

Diagnose before changing policy: record per-expert token counts and utilization, router scores and entropy, capacity-factor limits, overflow/dropped/padded tokens, queueing, expert compute time, dispatch/combine and all-to-all latency, network contention, placement/topology, batch composition, and synchronization. Check whether a hot expert is caused by a traffic slice, long sequences, correlated prompts, or an implementation imbalance rather than intrinsic routing.

Controlled experiment: replay randomized, representative, fixed-seed workloads with identical arrival rate and warm-up. Compare the current policy against one change at a time (for example capacity factor or load-balancing/routing policy), using matched replicas and repeated trials. Measure throughput and goodput, TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99/max latency, queue time, per-expert load, overflow/drop/padding, all-to-all and compute time, memory, network traffic, errors, and task-quality checks. Stratify by prompt length, batch size, and traffic slice; report confidence intervals and the full configuration. Confounders include cache state, autoscaling, co-tenants, network variability, kernel/compiler changes, warm-up, random seeds, and altered admission or completion accounting. Do not trade away correctness, privacy, or availability for lower tail latency. Roll back on quality regression, increased drops/errors, capacity or memory violations, SLO breach, or a statistically credible goodput regression; canary first and retain the prior policy.
risks: A routing-policy change can shift drops or quality while appearing to improve p99 latency.
Aggregate averages can hide hot experts and prompt-length or traffic-slice regressions.
Uncontrolled network, cache, autoscaling, or co-tenant effects can confound attribution.
evidence_required: Repeated matched replay with configuration and seed manifest.
Per-expert routing/capacity/drop/padding traces plus all-to-all, compute, queue, memory, and network telemetry.
Request-level latency, goodput, errors, and task-quality results stratified by workload slice with uncertainty estimates.
